related_questions.snippet: Towards the end, you may be sleepy or unconscious much of the time. You may also lose interest in eating and drinking. Your breathing pattern may change and eventually, your skin may become pale and moist, and you will become very drowsy. You may wish to consider end-of-life care.

related_questions.question: Can pulmonary fibrosis suddenly worsen?
related_questions.snippet: In some people, pulmonary fibrosis progresses very quickly, while for others their condition remains stable for many years. Some conditions progress at a steady rate. In others, apparently stable conditions can change suddenly. This sudden worsening of symptoms is called an exacerbation.

related_questions.question: What happens if you have scar tissue in your lungs?
related_questions.snippet: Scarred lung tissues have a hard time getting oxygen to the rest of your body and can make your heart work harder. This can lead to complications that include: Low oxygen in your blood (hypoxemia) and tissues (hypoxia) High blood pressure in your lungs (pulmonary hypertension)

related_questions.question: What is the life expectancy of a person with pulmonary fibrosis?

text_blocks.snippet: The average life expectancy for someone with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF), the most common type of pulmonary fibrosis, is typically 3-5 years after diagnosis, but this can vary significantly. While some individuals may experience a rapid decline and pass away within months, others can live for many years, even beyond 10 years.
snippet_highlighted_words: 3-5 years after diagnosis, but this can vary significantly

text_blocks.snippet: Several factors influence life expectancy for individuals with pulmonary fibrosis:

list.title: Type of Pulmonary Fibrosis:
list.snippet: IPF has a generally poorer prognosis compared to other types of pulmonary fibrosis, such as those caused by autoimmune diseases.

list.title: Age at Diagnosis and Overall Health:
list.snippet: Younger individuals with fewer pre-existing health conditions tend to have a better prognosis and longer survival rates.

list.title: Stage of Pulmonary Fibrosis:
list.snippet: The severity of lung damage at diagnosis (mild, moderate, severe, or very severe) significantly impacts life expectancy, with more advanced stages associated with shorter survival.

list.title: Treatment:
list.snippet: Anti-fibrotic medications like nintedanib and pirfenidone can slow down the progression of IPF and improve survival rates.

list.title: Individual Variability:
list.snippet: Lung function decline rates vary, and some individuals may experience more rapid progression than others.

list.title: Acute Exacerbations:
list.snippet: Sudden worsening of symptoms (acute exacerbations) can be life-threatening and significantly impact survival.

text_blocks.snippet: While population-based averages can be helpful, they don't accurately predict an individual's lifespan. According to the American Lung Association,, the variability in disease progression and individual responses to treatment means that some people with pulmonary fibrosis will live much longer than the average.

text_blocks.snippet: End-stage pulmonary fibrosis symptoms include persistent shortness of breath, even at rest, a persistent dry cough, extreme fatigue, and unintentional weight loss. Other symptoms may include aching muscles and joints, and clubbing of the fingers or toes. As the disease progresses, individuals may experience a decline in appetite, difficulty swallowing, and changes in breathing patterns, including noisy breathing and increased chest secretions. Eventually, they may experience drowsiness, decreased consciousness, and reduced interest in eating and drinking.
snippet_highlighted_words: persistent shortness of breath, even at rest, a persistent dry cough, extreme fatigue, and unintentional weight loss

list.snippet: Shortness of breath (dyspnea): This is the most prominent symptom, worsening over time and potentially occurring even at rest.
Dry cough: A persistent, non-productive cough is another common symptom.
Changes in breathing patterns: This can include rapid breathing, long pauses between breaths, and noisy, moist breathing due to increased chest secretions.
Blue or gray skin or nails (cyanosis): This can indicate low oxygen levels in the blood.
Extreme fatigue: This can significantly impact daily activities.
Unintentional weight loss: This is often linked to decreased appetite.
Aching muscles and joints: These can be a result of the body's response to the disease.
Clubbing of fingers or toes: This refers to the widening and rounding of the tips of the fingers or toes.
Decreased appetite and difficulty swallowing: As the disease progresses, these can become more pronounced.
Drowsiness and decreased consciousness: This is often seen as the disease nears its end.
Reduced interest in eating and drinking: This can lead to further weight loss and weakness.

list.title: Individual variation:
list.snippet: The progression and severity of symptoms can vary significantly from person to person.

list.title: Acute exacerbations:
list.snippet: Sudden worsening of symptoms can occur, sometimes related to infections or other illnesses, and can be life-threatening.

list.title: End-of-life care:
list.snippet: As the disease progresses, end-of-life care planning becomes crucial to manage symptoms and improve quality of life.
